nameStory: The 'prickly' in prickly wild rose comes from this plant's enthusiastic approach to self-defense — it's absolutely bristling with thorns and prickles along its stems. Unlike many roses that have just a few scattered thorns, this northern beauty is densely armed, earning it the alternative name 'bristly rose' for its particularly spiky personality.
description: Prickly wild rose is a hardy shrub that brings classic rose beauty to New England's cooler regions. This deciduous shrub typically grows 3-6 feet tall with arching, thorny stems that form dense thickets. In summer, it produces lovely pink five-petaled flowers that smell sweetly of traditional roses, followed by bright red rose hips in fall. It's one of our most northern-adapted wild roses, built to handle harsh winters.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Densely covered with straight, needle-like prickles of varying sizes — both large thorns and tiny bristles that feel rough to the touch, much more heavily armed than most other wild roses

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Classic five-petaled pink roses, 2-3 inches across, with the familiar sweet rose fragrance and a center full of yellow stamens

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 5-7 oval leaflets that have toothed edges and feel slightly fuzzy underneath when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red to orange rose hips about half an inch across that persist into winter, shaped like tiny tomatoes and feeling firm when squeezed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, sprawling thickets with arching canes that may root where they touch the ground, creating impenetrable thorny colonies

habitat: In New England, prickly wild rose favors cooler, northern locations and higher elevations where it can handle harsh winter conditions. Look for it along forest edges, in clearings, and on rocky slopes with well-drained soil. It's more likely to be found in northern New England's mountains and cooler valleys than in warmer southern areas.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as compound leaflets, and you can easily spot the densely prickly stems as the plant leafs out in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Pink roses bloom from June through July, filling the air with sweet fragrance and attracting bees and other pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Bright red rose hips ripen and the leaves may turn yellow before dropping, making the colorful hips stand out against bare thorny stems.
seasonality.winter: The dense thorny stems and persistent red hips make identification possible even in snow, creating winter interest in the landscape.

funFact: This tough little rose is actually the official flower of Alberta, Canada, and can survive temperatures down to -40°F — making it one of the most cold-hardy roses in the world, perfectly adapted to survive New England's harshest winters!
confusionNotes: The key to separating prickly wild rose from other wild roses is in the name — count the prickles! While swamp rose or Carolina rose might have thorns here and there, prickly wild rose looks like it's wearing a suit of armor with prickles covering nearly every inch of stem surface.
contextualKnowledge: With only 7 recorded observations in New England, prickly wild rose is quite rare in our region and represents the southern edge of its range here. You're much more likely to encounter it if you're hiking in northern New Hampshire or Vermont's mountains, where the climate better suits this Arctic-adapted species.
compareHints: Among New England's wild roses, prickly wild rose stands out for its extreme thorniness — it has far more prickles per inch than rugosa rose, swamp rose, or any of our other native roses. While rugosa rose has wrinkled leaves and larger hips, and swamp rose prefers wet areas, prickly wild rose's dense armament of straight prickles makes it unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England roses, multiflora rose is unique for its enormous flower clusters (other roses have flowers in smaller groups or singly) and those telltale fringed stipules.
Rugosa rose stands apart from other New England roses with its unmistakable wrinkled leaves - no other rose species has this corrugated texture.

Among New England's wild roses, swamp rose is unique in its preference for wet habitats - while Carolina rose and Virginia rose stick to drier areas, and multiflora rose (an invasive) has much denser thorns and forms larger, more aggressive colonies.
Among New England's wild roses, Carolina rose is the champion spreader, forming low colonies while relatives like swamp rose grow taller and more upright.
Among New England's wild roses, Virginian rose stands out for its glossy leaflets (rugosa rose has wrinkled leaves) and typically 7-9 leaflets per leaf (most others have fewer).

Among New England's roses, Sherard's downy-rose stands out for its compact size and distinctly grayish, downy leaves - most other wild roses like swamp rose or Carolina rose have greener, smoother foliage.

Among New England's wild roses, smooth rose is unique for its nearly thornless stems – multiflora rose has curved thorns, rugosa rose has dense straight prickles, and swamp rose has scattered thorns along its stems.
Among New England's roses, dog-rose stands out for its large, curved thorns and smooth leaflets without fuzzy coating.
Memorial rose is unique among New England roses for its prostrate, ground-hugging growth habit - all other rose species in the region grow as upright shrubs.
Among New England's wild roses, shining rose is uniquely low-growing and has by far the glossiest leaves.
Unlike the common multiflora rose with its clusters of small white flowers, cinnamon rose has larger, solitary pink blooms.
Among New England's roses, sweet-brier is the only one with apple-scented leaves - this fragrance alone separates it from multiflora rose, rugosa rose, and native species.
Climbing prairie rose stands out from other New England roses primarily by its vigorous climbing habit with long, flexible canes.
Unlike New England's native roses such as swamp rose or Carolina rose which have green leaves, red-leaved rose's blue-gray to purplish foliage is unmistakable.
